title: Abba (Mark 14:32–52)
hook: he calls God by the family word, and a young man flees leaving his linen cloth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the upper room: bread and cup, and one word, take. Your line was take. What did you accept without refusing? After supper they walked out to the Mount of Olives. Today, the garden. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

Most of us have had one night we'd never want to live again. Waiting for a phone call. Sitting by a bed. Today is that night for Jesus. They come to a place called Gethsemane, an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives. The name probably means oil press. He tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, takes Peter, James and John further in, and Mark says he began to be terrified and deeply troubled. He tells them his soul is sorrowful even unto death. Stay here and watch. Then he goes a little further alone, and falls on the ground.
screen: `THE WORST NIGHT.` → `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.` → `HE FALLS ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Face down in the dirt, he prays, in the Douay-Rheims: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee: remove this chalice from me; but not what I will, but what thou wilt." Abba is Aramaic, the everyday word for father used inside a family. Mark keeps the sound, then translates it. You'll sometimes hear that abba means daddy. Scholars now say that's too cute: grown children called their fathers abba too. It's not baby talk. It's close, trusting, family speech, at the worst moment of his life. Second, the honesty. He asks for the cup to pass. He doesn't pretend to want it. And then he hands the choice back: not my will, yours. Catholics see here both his true human fear and his free obedience. Third, the sleepers. He comes back three times and finds them asleep. Remember the last word of his speech two days ago: watch. "Watch ye, and pray that you enter not into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak." Fourth, the arrest. Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and greets Jesus with a kiss. Someone draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. And then, Mark says, they all left him and fled. One more detail that only Mark tells. A young man was following, wearing only a linen cloth. They grab him, and he leaves the cloth in their hands and runs away naked. Nobody knows who he was. An old guess says it was Mark himself, signing his Gospel. The sources don't say.
screen: `ABBA: THE FAMILY WORD FOR FATHER.` · `REMOVE THIS CHALICE. NOT MY WILL.` · `ASLEEP THREE TIMES. WATCH AND PRAY.` · `A KISS, A SWORD, AND THEY ALL FLED.` · then, large: `ABBA, FATHER, ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray to God as Abba, or sit with the word. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind the thing you most wish would pass from you right now. Say honestly that you don't want it. Then, if you pray, you can use Jesus's own words: Abba, Father. Just those two, slowly, on your breath, as many times as you need. If you don't pray, think of the person whose voice feels most like home, and let yourself rest in that for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Abba. Aramaic for father, the word used inside a family. Jesus says it face down in Gethsemane, the night before he dies. Today's word.
Your line: abba, father. Today, when you're afraid of something, say it honestly first, to God or to someone you trust, before you pretend you're fine. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 227 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BEFORE THE COCK CROWS TWICE.`

howItsDone: On Holy Thursday night many Catholic parishes keep watch before the Blessed Sacrament until midnight, remembering Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, and the Agony in the Garden is the first Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary.

original.note: Aramaic abba, then the Greek for the father: Mark keeps the word and translates it.

trapdoor: what you thought: abba means daddy.
what it means: the everyday Aramaic word for father, said in fear and trust at once: not my will, but yours.
what a scholar hears: an Aramaic word kept in a Greek Gospel, which Paul also uses in Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6; the daddy claim is now widely doubted.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 14:36 and 14:38 given from memory; confirm.

Gethsemane from Aramaic/Hebrew gat shemanim, 'oil press': 'probably' kept. Confirm.
The identification of the young man with Mark is an old conjecture, flagged as a guess.
The rest of the Mark 14:32–52 details (kiss, sword, flight) summarized; confirm. Holy Thursday watch and the Sorrowful Mysteries in howItsDone: confirm.
